title: The Birthright Sold for Books: Warburg, the Hopi Mesas, and the Atlas of Memory
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Hamburg, birth into the banking house
stops.date_confidence: attested date; the family address is approximate, placed in the Rothenbaum and Harvestehude district
stops.campa: In a house of the Warburg banking family, whose credit has served Hamburg's trade for generations, a first son is born and named Aby Moritz. Six more children will follow him. The firm M.M. Warburg & Co. expects the eldest to take it over in his turn; the ledgers are the family scripture and the harbor outside is what the ledgers are about. He will refuse that inheritance for sixty years without ever leaving the money behind. What the firm earns he spends on photographs and on books by the shelf. The question he spends it to answer is why a painted gesture outlives the century that made it.
suggested_refs: The counting house of M.M. Warburg & Co. on the Ferdinandstrasse, Hamburg
sources: E.H. Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography (1970)

stops.name: Bad Ischl, the lending library and the sausages
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The boy is eight, sent to the Salzkammergut spa town in the year of his mother's severe illness. Two diversions hold him there: a small lending library whose stories of Red Indians he devours in masses, and a grocery where he gorges on sausages no kosher table at home would permit. Looking back as a grown man he calls the pair of them his inoculation against active cruelty. Both appetites survive intact. Twenty-two years later he will go to Arizona to find the people the lending library had invented for him, and will find them entirely real.
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, of the Red Indian tales and the sausages at Bad Ischl, cited in E.H. Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography, 19-20
suggested_refs: The small lending library at Bad Ischl, source of Warburg's first Indians
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography, 19-20
Kevin Dann, 'Warburg's Werewolf: An Anamnesis', Public Domain Review

stops.name: Hamburg, the bargain with Max
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the family anecdote is dated to his thirteenth year and no source cites a contemporary document
stops.campa: At thirteen he makes his younger brother Max an offer: Max may have the birthright, the firm, the seat at the head of the table, on one condition, that he buy Aby every book he ever asks for. Max accepts. Neither of them yet knows the size of the debt. The books will outgrow a study, then a house, then two houses joined. In the end they take a purpose-built library with an oval reading room, a staff to run it, and a ship to get them out of Germany. The Warburgs keep the bargain to the end, on a promise made by a boy who wanted to read.
stops.quote: was certainly the most careless [business decision] of my life
stops.quote_source: Max Warburg on the childhood pact, quoted in Emily J. Levine, 'A Hamburg Friendship: Erwin Panofsky's Obituary on Aby Warburg', Key Documents of German-Jewish History; Max repeated the confession at Aby's memorial service, per Michael P. Steinberg's afterword to the Cornell edition, 76 and 111
suggested_refs: The family anecdote of the birthright, recorded by Warburg's biographers
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Bonn, Usener and the comparative method
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted; coordinates are the university main building
stops.campa: He enrolls at Bonn to read art history, history and archaeology, sitting under Carl Justi and Henry Thode. The teacher who marks him is not an art historian at all: Hermann Usener, historian of religion, who follows a single motif across languages and centuries and treats a survival as evidence rather than as ornament. Karl Lamprecht teaches him in the same years a cultural history that reaches past kings into custom and belief. Connoisseurship leaves him cold, and he will decline to play that game for forty years.
suggested_refs: Hermann Usener's comparative religious philology at Bonn
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Florence, the circle around August Schmarsow
stops.date_confidence: winter semester 1888-89 attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He comes to Florence to work among the pictures his thesis depends on, and joins the study circle August Schmarsow holds in his own apartments and calls a Kunsthistorisches Institut: no building, no charter, nine students, Max J. Friedlander and Hermann Ulmann among them. The institute of that name is not founded until 1897, under Heinrich Brockhaus. What exists in 1888 is a handful of Germans reading each other's notes in a foreign city, and Warburg spending his days in front of quattrocento paintings arguing about what a painting is evidence of.
suggested_refs: Schmarsow's Florentine seminar of 1888-89, called retrospectively the founding act of the Kunsthistorisches Institut
sources: Uffizi.it, 'Rooms with a View: Aby Warburg, Florence and the Laboratory of Images'

stops.name: Florence, the Uffizi and the moving hair
stops.date_confidence: inferred within the 1888-89 Florence stay; month not documented
stops.campa: In the Uffizi he stands before the Birth of Venus and the Primavera, the two pictures his dissertation turns on. He is not there to praise them. He wants to know why Venus's hair lifts as it does, why Flora's drapery moves against a still garden, why a Christian city reaches back past its own centuries for figures caught in antique motion. The answer he begins assembling is that the movement is quoted rather than observed: Botticelli has taken it from maenads and nymphs on Roman sarcophagi, without needing to know that he has.
suggested_refs: Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera, Galleria degli Uffizi
sources: Aby Warburg, Sandro Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Spring (1893)

stops.name: Strasbourg, the Botticelli dissertation
stops.date_confidence: year of the defence attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Hubert Janitschek at the Kaiser-Wilhelms-Universitat lets him write the thesis no safer supervisor would have allowed, and in 1892 he defends it. Its argument is small and its consequences are not: the flying hair and flying garments of Botticelli's figures descend from antique models of movement, and the painters using them inherit a formula for feeling rather than invent one. Published the following year, it holds in miniature everything he will spend thirty-seven more years enlarging. The word for the thing, Pathosformel, has not been coined yet.
suggested_refs: Warburg's 1893 printed dissertation on the Birth of Venus and Spring
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Berlin, two semesters of medicine
stops.date_confidence: two semesters attested for 1892-93, after the doctorate and not before it; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: After the doctorate he does what an art historian is not supposed to do: he enrolls at the medical faculty in Berlin for two semesters and sits through lectures on psychology and the nervous system. He wants to know how a body produces fear and ecstasy, not only how a painter renders them. The detour looks like restlessness and is in fact the whole program, an art history that treats images as biological events. Thirty years on, in a Swiss clinic, doctors will find their patient answering them in something uncomfortably close to their own vocabulary.
stops.quote: Die formale Betrachtung des Bildes – unbegriffen als biologisch notwendiges Produkt zwischen Religion und Kunstausübung – [...] schien mir ein steriles Wortgeschäft hervorzurufen [...]
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, recalling his motive for undertaking fieldwork; quoted in German Wikipedia, 'Aby Warburg', after the Gesammelte Schriften and Gombrich. Translation: the formal consideration of the image, not understood as a biologically necessary product between religion and artistic practice, seemed to me to provoke a sterile business of words
suggested_refs: The medical faculty of the University of Berlin, 1892-93
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: New York, his brother Paul's wedding
stops.date_confidence: autumn 1895 attested for the crossing and the wedding; day defaulted, and no source names the venue
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic for a family occasion, his brother Paul's marriage to Nina Loeb, the kind of Warburg errand he has spent his adult life sidestepping. New York is the American branch of the family's world: banking again, marriages again, the same conversation in a different harbor. He discharges the obligation and then does not go home. The continent behind the city has ethnographers in it, and pueblos, and a ceremonial life no European library holds. He buys a camera and turns west with no institution asking him to.
suggested_refs: Paul Warburg's 1895 New York wedding, the errand that opened the Southwest
sources: Southwest Contemporary, review of Uwe Fleckner, 'The Snake and the Lightning'

stops.name: Washington, the Smithsonian ethnologists
stops.date_confidence: inferred within late 1895; one account places the Smithsonian weeks in December, and no source gives a day
stops.campa: At the Smithsonian he seeks out the men who have actually lived in the country he means to enter: James Mooney, who has studied the Ghost Dance, Frank Hamilton Cushing, who spent years among the Zuni, and beside them Jesse Walter Fewkes and Franz Boas. They give him letters, contacts, and a working vocabulary: kiva, kachina, the names of villages and the names of what happens inside them. He takes the vocabulary seriously enough to be still using it three decades later, in front of a room of psychiatrists, arguing that Athens and Oraibi think in the same way.
suggested_refs: The Bureau of American Ethnology at the Smithsonian, Warburg's point of entry
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Santa Fe, Cleo Jurino draws the world-house
stops.date_confidence: attested; Warburg's own lecture text names the hotel room and the date
stops.campa: Santa Fe is where the railroad stops being scenery and the fieldwork begins: an old Spanish plaza, letters from the Smithsonian men in his pocket, a camera he has not yet used on anybody. On the tenth of January, in room 59 of the Palace Hotel, a kiva priest of Cochiti named Cleo Jurino and his son Anacleto sit down with his paper and colored pencils and draw the world-house: the stepped sky, the serpent, the rain the serpent commands. He came for the survivals of antiquity and is handed a working cosmology by two men who still use it.
stops.quote: The actual village lies on the far side of the Atchison-Topeka-Santa Fe railway line.
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians of North America, trans. Michael P. Steinberg (Cornell University Press, 1995), 5, on the pueblo settlements seen from the railroad; spoken in 1923 about the 1895-96 journey
suggested_refs: The drawings of the world-house made for Warburg by Cleo Jurino and Anacleto at Santa Fe, 10 January 1896
sources: Warburg, Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians of North America (Cornell UP, 1995)
Warburg Institute Archive, 'Aby Warburg's Pueblo Materials'

stops.name: San Ildefonso Pueblo, the antelope dance
stops.date_confidence: early 1896 attested, month inferred; coordinates are the pueblo plaza
stops.campa: At San Ildefonso on the Rio Grande he photographs the antelope dance and the kiva architecture, filling notebooks with lightning zigzags and serpent forms in the way another man would note the fall of a drapery. He is an outsider with a camera among people who owe him nothing, and the position troubles later scholars more than it troubles him. What he takes away is evidence for something he already half believes. Symbolic thought does not evolve out of magic and leave it behind; it changes address and goes on working.
suggested_refs: Warburg's 1895-96 photographic plates, Warburg Institute Archive
sources: Warburg Institute Archive, Warburg's 1895-96 photographs and diary
English Wikipedia, 'San Ildefonso Pueblo, New Mexico'

stops.name: Acoma Pueblo, the climb to the Sky City
stops.date_confidence: early 1896 attested by Warburg's own list of the pueblo plazas he stood on; month inferred
stops.campa: Acoma stands on a mesa three hundred and sixty-seven feet above the plain, reachable in 1896 only by hand and foot up steps cut in the rock. Warburg makes the climb. On the plaza at the top is a village whose people chose this stone precisely because nothing here could be taken from them easily, and a mission church raised by Spanish order over ceremonial ground that never stopped being used. The difficulty of the ascent is not an obstacle to what he came for. It is the argument itself: distance is one of the things that lets a form survive.
suggested_refs: The Sky City mesa at Acoma and the mission church of San Esteban del Rey

stops.name: Zuni Pueblo, in Cushing's village
stops.date_confidence: early 1896 attested; month and day inferred within the New Mexico leg
stops.campa: Zuni is the village Frank Hamilton Cushing lived inside for years before writing it into the reports Warburg read in Washington, so arriving here is like walking into a book already annotated. Terraced adobe, a governor and bow priests, rain societies with a serpent of their own, a religion running in daylight. He photographs, buys pottery, fills a notebook. What he carries away from Zuni will sit uncatalogued for decades among Pueblo materials that travel from his house in Hamburg to a London institute he does not live to see.
stops.quote: To us, this synchrony of fantastic magic and sober purposiveness appears as a symptom of a cleavage; for the Indian this is not schizoid but, rather, a liberating experience of the boundless communicability between man and environment.
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians of North America, trans. Michael P. Steinberg (Cornell University Press, 1995), 2
suggested_refs: Warburg's Pueblo collection, Warburg Institute Archive, London

stops.name: Mesa Verde, the Cliff Palace
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested; the length of the stop is disputed among biographers and the month is undocumented
stops.campa: The cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde are already a fixture of the American tourist imagination by the time his route crosses Colorado. Whether he stops here at length or only passes near it is not settled in the surviving diary fragments, and the biographers disagree. What is clear is how well the abandoned stone rooms fit the argument he is assembling everywhere on this journey. A people's symbols outlast the people. The rooms stand empty and still legible, and the images they were built around are being handled a hundred miles south.
suggested_refs: Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde, on the winter 1895-96 itinerary
sources: Secondary biographical accounts, itinerary disputed among Warburg scholars

stops.name: Keams Canyon, the missionary Voth
stops.date_confidence: inferred within the spring 1896 Hopi stay; month and day not documented
stops.campa: He reaches Hopi country and stays at Keams Canyon, in the company of Heinrich Richert Voth, the Mennonite missionary whose ethnography of Hopi ceremony is as thorough as his intention to end it. Warburg takes his access from a man working to abolish what he is recording, and there is no sign the arrangement troubles him at the time. From here he goes up onto the mesas with photographic plates, into villages that have received very few Europeans and have no reason to make it easy for one more.
stops.quote: the Indian children go to school in comely suits and pinafores and no longer believe in pagan demons
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians of North America, trans. Michael P. Steinberg (Cornell University Press, 1995), 50
suggested_refs: H.R. Voth's Hopi ethnographic collections, gathered while converting the people described

stops.name: Walpi, First Mesa
stops.date_confidence: spring 1896 attested, day defaulted within the Hopi stay; the snake dance is an August ceremony and he was present at none
stops.campa: Walpi stands on the tip of First Mesa, stone houses on a cliff edge above a desert that runs to the horizon. He climbs to it and photographs what he is permitted to photograph, taking notes in an art historian's terms: composition, rhythm, repetition, applied to a ceremony instead of a fresco. The snake dance is danced in August and he is here in spring; the plates of it he keeps for the rest of his life were made by other men. He leaves with the outer skin of something closed to him, and twenty-seven years in which to decide what it was evidence of.
stops.quote: They stand on middle ground between magic and logos, and their instrument of orientation is the symbol.
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians of North America, trans. Michael P. Steinberg (Cornell University Press, 1995), 17
suggested_refs: Warburg's photographs of Walpi, First Mesa, and the purchased plates of the Walpi snake dance

stops.name: Oraibi, Third Mesa
stops.date_confidence: attested, 28 April to 1 May 1896; the dance he watched was a Hemis kachina, and his eyewitness presence at a serpent ceremony is contested
stops.campa: Oraibi on Third Mesa is his furthest and last Hopi stop, reached in the last days of April. Between the twenty-eighth and the first of May he watches a Hemis kachina dance, with the missionary Voth speaking for him where he cannot speak for himself. This village becomes the anchor of the lecture he gives twenty-seven years later in a Swiss clinic, in which Athens and Oraibi are held to be cousins out of one old book. David Freedberg's later charge is not that Warburg lied about Oraibi. It is that he did not see what was in front of him.
stops.quote: Es ist ein altes Buch zu blättern, Athen-Oraibi, alles Vettern.
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg's own German verse, epigraph to Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians of North America, trans. Michael P. Steinberg (Cornell University Press, 1995), 1, rendered by that edition as: It is a lesson from an old book, the kinship of Athens and Oraibi
suggested_refs: Old Oraibi, Third Mesa, and the disputed eyewitness claim
sources: Philippe-Alain Michaud, Aby Warburg and the Image in Motion

stops.name: Hamburg, home with the plates
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the year of return is attested, the month is not
stops.campa: He sails home with photographic plates, Hopi and Pueblo objects, and a theory he cannot yet say out loud. Hamburg receives him as a curiosity, the Warburg son who went to look at Indians instead of touring cathedrals. The objects go eventually to the city's ethnographic museum; about the journey itself he publishes almost nothing. It sits in him unspent for twenty-seven years while he becomes a Renaissance scholar of formidable reputation, until circumstances no one could have designed force it out of him in front of an audience of psychiatric patients.
suggested_refs: The unpublished American material, held back from 1896 to 1923
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

segments.name: Florence, Where the Theory Becomes a Method

stops.name: Hamburg, marriage to Mary Hertz
stops.date_confidence: year attested; exact wedding date and venue not verified beyond secondary biography
stops.campa: He marries Mary Hertz, daughter of a Hamburg senator, a trained painter and sculptor who will make coins and medals and argue with him about form as an equal. His father opposes the match because she is not Jewish. Aby marries her anyway, which is the second inheritance he declines. Three children follow: Marietta, Max Adolph, Frede Charlotte. Mary's own work recedes under the weight of his, the ordinary Hamburg bargain of the period, and her eye stays visible in what he chooses to keep looking at for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Mary Warburg's sculpture and medal work, largely eclipsed by the library
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Florence, the household near Piazzale Donatello
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the residential address is approximate, not independently confirmed
stops.campa: The couple settles in Florence for four years, close to the archives and the paintings the work depends on. Here he writes on Ghirlandaio and Botticelli, and the theory hardens into a method: a stock gesture of extreme feeling, flying hair, flying drapery, the raised arm, recurs from antique relief into quattrocento painting because painters learn emotion from earlier images and not only from bodies. Marietta is born in the first year. Of the three cities that have a claim on him, this is the one he assigns to his soul.
stops.quote: Ebreo di sangue, Amburghese di cuore, d'anima Fiorentino
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg's short autobiographical phrase in Italian, recorded by Gertrud Bing, 'Aby M. Warburg', Rivista storica italiana (1960), 113, and taken as its title by engramma no. 2662; the attested order is blood, then Hamburg, then Florence
suggested_refs: Warburg's Ghirlandaio essays, written in the Florentine years
sources: Bing, Rivista storica italiana (1960), 113, via engramma.it no. 2662
Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Florence, Ghirlandaio in the Sassetti Chapel
stops.date_confidence: within the 1898-1902 Florentine years; the essays appear across the following decade, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In the Sassetti Chapel at Santa Trinita he reads Ghirlandaio's frescoes as documents rather than devotions. Behind Saint Francis the painter has put the actual Piazza della Signoria, the Palazzo Vecchio, and living Florentines in their own clothes standing among the sacred figures; the banker Francesco Sassetti has bought himself a place inside biblical time. Warburg counts the faces, matches them against names in ledgers, and treats the painting as a receipt for a transaction between a merchant house and eternity.
suggested_refs: Ghirlandaio's Sassetti Chapel frescoes at Santa Trinita, and the Tornabuoni choir at Santa Maria Novella
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Florence, the Archivio di Stato
stops.date_confidence: the Florentine archival research is attested for these years; individual sessions are undated and the month is defaulted
stops.campa: He spends his hours not in front of the frescoes but underneath them, in the state archive, reading merchant account books, wedding inventories, tax returns, the paper of the Medici circle and its clients. A Ghirlandaio fresco, he decides, explains less than the invoice for the dress painted into it. This is where art history stops being about masterpieces for him. The picture becomes a document of a culture's whole business: its debts, its marriages, its astrological fears. The ledgers he refused at thirteen come back to him as evidence.
suggested_refs: The Archivio di Stato di Firenze, source of Warburg's Florentine account-book research
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Hamburg, the family comes home
stops.date_confidence: contested: Wikipedia gives 1902, warburg-haus.de gives 1904. Max Adolph is born in Florence in 1902 and Frede Charlotte in Hamburg in 1904, which fits the later date better. Left unresolved
stops.campa: The Warburgs return to Hamburg and the library that has been travelling in crates comes back with them. Max Adolph is born the same year, Frede Charlotte two years later. Aby is a private scholar with no post, no students and no institution, supported by the bank he handed away, and the arrangement suits him precisely. What he is building has neither a name nor an address yet. It is simply understood in the city that if a book is not to be found in Hamburg, it is probably in Warburg's house.
suggested_refs: The Warburg private library before it had a name
sources: Fritz Saxl, memorial essays on Warburg

stops.name: Hamburg, the calendar of Stephan Arndes
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He lectures on the calendar printed by Stephan Arndes and turns toward astrology, which for him is not a curiosity of superstition but the exact place where antiquity survives into the modern world. The zodiac is a machine for carrying pagan gods through a Christian millennium in disguise, and men who would burn an idol will consult its decans without noticing what they are handling. He begins collecting almanacs, prognostications, star charts. The library drifts away from anything a museum would recognize as art.
stops.quote: Athens wants again and again to be reconquered afresh from Alexandria.
stops.quote_source: Warburg's dictum, from the Luther essay of 1920, German: Athen will eben immer wieder neu aus Alexandrien zuruckerobert sein. This English wording is quoted in Emily J. Levine, 'A Hamburg Friendship', keydocuments.net; Steinberg's afterword to the Cornell edition, 69 and 88, renders it: Athens always wants precisely to be reconquered anew from Alexandria
suggested_refs: The Stephan Arndes calendar and Warburg's astrological collection
sources: Steinberg, afterword to Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians (Cornell UP, 1995)

stops.name: Hamburg, Heilwigstrasse 114
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The collection moves into Heilwigstrasse 114 and becomes, without ceremony, the Kulturwissenschaftliche Bibliothek Warburg. It is shelved on a principle he calls the good neighbor: books placed so that the volume standing beside the one you came for answers the question you had not yet thought to ask. Subject headings are refused as a form of premature conclusion. In 1912 Halle offers him a professorial chair and he declines it; the Hamburg Senate confers a professor's title on him instead, and he keeps his freedom and his shelves.
suggested_refs: The good neighbor shelving principle, still the ordering rule of the Warburg Institute

stops.name: Ferrara, the Salone dei Mesi
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the research is dated to 1912, the specific visit is not
stops.campa: Under the frescoed months of the Salone dei Mesi at Palazzo Schifanoia he works out a puzzle earlier art historians had shelved as decoration. The strange figures banded across each month are not Ferrarese invention. They are astrological decans, transmitted from Babylon through Arabic and medieval Latin sources into a fifteenth-century Italian court, and he matches them one by one to their texts. Nobody in Ferrara could still read them correctly when they were painted, and they were painted anyway.
stops.quote: the pagan augur who assumed the mantle of scientific learning was a hard adversary to contend with, let alone to defeat
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, 'Pagan-Antique Prophecy in Words and Images in the Age of Luther' (1920), trans. David Britt, in The Renewal of Pagan Antiquity (Getty Research Institute, 1999), as quoted in the HASTA article 'Aby Warburg, Distance, and Meaning-Making in the American Southwest'; written eight years after the Schifanoia work
suggested_refs: The Salone dei Mesi, Palazzo Schifanoia, Ferrara
sources: Aby Warburg, 'Italian Art and International Astrology in the Palazzo Schifanoia, Ferrara' (1912)
Warburg, 'Pagan-Antique Prophecy in Words and Images in the Age of Luther' (1920)

stops.name: Rome, the Tenth International Congress
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: At the Tenth International Congress of the History of Art he reads the Schifanoia paper to a room of specialists. He has shown that images travel across religions, languages and a thousand years, and that they arrive carrying meanings their own patrons no longer understand. To follow one such route takes astrology, philology and Arabic manuscripts as much as an eye for quality. It is the lecture that makes his name among people who had taken him for an eccentric private collector.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the Tenth International Congress of the History of Art, Rome 1912
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography
Warburg, 'Italian Art and International Astrology in the Palazzo Schifanoia, Ferrara' (1912)

stops.name: Hamburg, the war-news archive
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the war years; the archive's start month is not documented
stops.campa: When the war comes he turns the library into a war archive, clipping newspapers from every belligerent, filing propaganda images beside classical ones, tracking how modern states reach for antique symbols in order to justify killing. The work is compulsive as much as scholarly. Visitors notice that the connections arrive faster than any argument can hold them, and when Germany loses in 1918 something gives way in the man who has spent four years reading the whole catastrophe as iconography.
suggested_refs: The KBW wartime press-cutting archive, 1914-1918
sources: Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Hamburg, November 1918
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: With revolution in the streets and the empire finished, the collapse arrives in full. He is convinced of catastrophe, convinced of conspiracies against him, and at the worst of it he threatens his own family with a weapon. Among the hallucinations that begin this year is one he will later describe without embarrassment: that he is turning into a werewolf. The scholar who spent twenty years arguing that antique terror survives inside modern images is now inhabited by one, and is able to report the process from the inside.
stops.quote: fear aroused by the incoherence and the disproportionate force of visual memories
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, 'Anamnesis', University of Tübingen historical archive UAT 441/3782, reproduced in Binswanger and Warburg, La guérison infinie (Paris: Rivages, 2020), 189-194
suggested_refs: Dr Herbert Embden's note on the onset of the werewolf hallucinations in 1918
sources: Binswanger and Warburg, La guerison infinie (Paris: Rivages, 2020), 88
Kevin Dann, 'Warburg's Werewolf: An Anamnesis', Public Domain Review

stops.name: Hamburg, the clinics and the new university
stops.date_confidence: 1919 is the founding year of the university; the professor's title itself dates from 1912 and only now attaches to an institution. The names of the private clinics are in no reachable source
stops.campa: A run of private clinics in and around Hamburg attempts treatment and fails; their names are not specified in reachable sources. In the same year the city founds its university at last, and the title the Senate gave him in 1912 finally attaches to an actual institution. His library becomes on paper a research institute of a university he is in no state to enter. Fritz Saxl holds the place together; Erwin Panofsky arrives in 1920 and finds an institution running in its founder's absence, on his shelving and his questions.
suggested_refs: The KBW under Saxl's direction during Warburg's absence, 1919-1924

stops.name: Kreuzlingen, admission to Bellevue
stops.date_confidence: attested; the admitting diagnosis at Binswanger's clinic is schizophrenia
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of April he is admitted to the Sanatorium Bellevue at Kreuzlingen, on the Swiss shore of Lake Constance, the private clinic of Ludwig Binswanger, a psychiatrist unusual in his willingness to attend to the inner logic of a delusion instead of merely suppressing it. The clinic writes down schizophrenia, which in 1921 means no return. Two weeks in, the nurse Friede Hecht records what her patient keeps shouting. The family that could afford any clinic in Europe has bought the one physician likely to listen to it.
stops.quote: I am going to be a werewolf! I am a werewolf!
stops.quote_source: Nurse Friede Hecht's clinical record, circa late April 1921; Binswanger and Warburg, La guerison infinie (Paris: Rivages, 2020), 77-78
suggested_refs: Binswanger's clinical file on Warburg, published as La guarigione infinita and La guerison infinie
sources: Kevin Dann, 'Warburg's Werewolf: An Anamnesis', Public Domain Review

stops.name: Kreuzlingen, Kraepelin revises the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted; the consultation belongs to 1923 and not, as some accounts have it, to the admission of 1921
stops.campa: Emil Kraepelin, whose classification of the psychoses is the ground the whole profession stands on, is brought in and overturns the schizophrenia diagnosis in favor of a mixed manic-depressive state with a good prognosis. The distinction is not academic. Schizophrenia in 1923 means no return; manic depression means episodes, and episodes end. Binswanger's correspondence in these years runs to Vienna and Sigmund Freud, so the case is being argued inside the small circle where European psychiatry is still deciding what a mind is.
stops.quote: Umburri, umburri, umburri. Meichucks . . . meichirix umbarigaisch umbarrigasch . . .
stops.quote_source: Nurse's clinical record of Warburg's speech during the breakdown; Binswanger and Warburg, La guérison infinie (Paris: Rivages, 2020), 77-78, quoted in Kevin Dann, 'Warburg's Werewolf: An Anamnesis', Public Domain Review
suggested_refs: Kraepelin's 1923 consultation and the revised diagnosis

stops.name: Kreuzlingen, images from the Pueblo country
stops.date_confidence: attested; the tradition that Binswanger set the lecture as a condition of release is later mythologising, since Warburg proposed it himself and was not discharged for sixteen months
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of April he stands up in front of doctors, nurses and fellow patients and delivers a lecture titled Bilder aus dem Gebiet der Pueblo-Indianer in Nord-Amerika, built from photographs and notes twenty-seven years old. He argues a kinship between religious thinking in Athens and in Oraibi, between the serpents of Laocoon and those of a Hopi dancer. It is also an examination he has set for himself: if he can hold an argument together in front of witnesses, he is a man who can be let out.
stops.quote: The masked dance is danced causality.
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians of North America, trans. Michael P. Steinberg (Cornell University Press, 1995), 48
suggested_refs: The lecture published posthumously as 'A Lecture on Serpent Ritual', Journal of the Warburg Institute 2 (1939), and in German as Schlangenritual (1988)
sources: Southwest Contemporary, 'Journey to the Origin of Images'
Kevin Dann, 'Warburg's Werewolf: An Anamnesis', Public Domain Review

stops.name: Kreuzlingen, the letter of 9 November
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: News reaches the sanatorium from Munich, where Ludendorff and a party agitator named Hitler have tried to seize a state in an afternoon. Warburg writes to Mary the same day. The clinical file of this same year records the same man producing syllables that mean nothing at all. The letter records him naming, on the afternoon it happens, what has just walked into German politics. He is a certified madman and one of the very few Germans of 1923 to read the news correctly, and both facts are on file at Kreuzlingen.
stops.quote: Ludendorff should be kept in a lunatic asylum and Hitler should be hanged!
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg to Mary Warburg, Warburg Institute Correspondence Files, WIA GC/37162, 9 November 1923
suggested_refs: WIA GC/37162, the Beer Hall Putsch letter
sources: Kevin Dann, 'Warburg's Werewolf: An Anamnesis', Public Domain Review, citing WIA GC/37162

stops.name: Kreuzlingen, released
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: He leaves Bellevue in August 1924 after three years and four months, judged fit for ordinary life, with Binswanger keeping a discreet lifelong interest in the case and eventually publishing it. There is no record of a later relapse. He returns to Hamburg quieter, still capable of the leaps that made the early work startling. Five years remain, and he can feel them going. He spends them building the one thing his whole method has been pointing at, an argument made almost entirely of pictures.
suggested_refs: Binswanger's published case history of his most famous patient
sources: ResearchGate, 'Aby Warburg, the Hopi Serpent Ritual and Ludwig Binswanger'
Gombrich, Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography

stops.name: Hamburg, the atlas begun
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested by the German sources; English accounts date the atlas to December 1927, which is the start of the systematic panel campaign rather than of the work
stops.campa: Back among his own shelves he begins Mnemosyne, named for the mother of the Muses, memory herself. It is a picture atlas: photographic reproductions of paintings, reliefs, coins, manuscript pages, postage stamps and newspaper cuttings, pinned to large panels covered in black cloth and arranged into constellations that trace the survival of antiquity. Nothing is glued down. The whole apparatus is built to be taken apart and recomposed, and that is as much of the argument as any single panel carries.
stops.quote: Human culture evolves towards reason in the same measure as the tangible fullness of life fades toward a mathematical symbol.
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, A Lecture on Serpent Ritual (Kreuzlingen, 1923), as quoted in the HASTA article 'Aby Warburg, Distance, and Meaning-Making in the American Southwest'
suggested_refs: Bilderatlas Mnemosyne, begun August 1924

stops.name: Hamburg, the oval reading room
stops.date_confidence: attested; opened 1 May 1926 with an inaugural address by Ernst Cassirer
stops.campa: On the first of May the purpose-built library opens next door at Heilwigstrasse 116, designed by Gerhard Langmaack on the recommendation of the city's chief building director Fritz Schumacher, its reading room an ellipse so that the shelves curve around the reader instead of ranking him down a corridor. Ernst Cassirer gives the inaugural address. Fritz Saxl and Gertrud Bing run the daily work; the founder presides, sometimes fragile, over an institution that now has staff, a lecture series and a publishing programme.
suggested_refs: The Warburg-Haus at Heilwigstrasse 116, Langmaack's elliptical reading room

stops.name: Hamburg, the panel campaign
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested for the systematic campaign, day defaulted; sources disagree on whether this is a start or a resumption
stops.campa: From December he works at the panels systematically, and the atlas takes the shape it will be remembered in. The counts drift between sources: over forty panels carrying somewhere between fifteen hundred and two thousand photographs at one stage, sixty-three panels and nine hundred and seventy-one images in the last state anyone photographed. He rearranges them continually and stops at no final version, so the record has nothing fixed to count. A final version would contradict what the thing is for.
stops.quote: The modern Prometheus and the modern Icarus, Franklin and the Wright brothers, who invented the dirigible airplane, are precisely those ominous destroyers of the sense of distance, who threaten to lead the planet back into chaos. Telegram and telephone destroy the cosmos.
stops.quote_source: Aby Warburg, Images from the Region of the Pueblo Indians of North America, trans. Michael P. Steinberg (Cornell University Press, 1995), 54, the closing passage of the Kreuzlingen lecture
suggested_refs: The surviving photographic record of the Mnemosyne panels in their 1929 state

stops.name: Rome, the Vatican Library
stops.date_confidence: inferred within the nine-month Italian journey of 1928-29; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He spends nine months in Italy with Gertrud Bing, working through the Vatican Library's manuscripts and the city's churches and villas for astrological and mythological survivals to feed the panels. He moves faster than his assistants can follow, sending material north to Hamburg as quickly as Rome yields it up. He is sixty-two years old, four years out of a psychiatric clinic, and running an image-gathering campaign across a country as though another twenty years were available to spend on it.
suggested_refs: Gertrud Bing's records of the 1928-29 Italian journey; Warburg's Diario romano
sources: Philippe-Alain Michaud, Aby Warburg and the Image in Motion

stops.name: Hamburg, the heart attack
stops.date_confidence: attested; his last written ordering of the panels is dated 19 October 1929, seven days earlier
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of October he dies of a heart attack, sixty-three years old, and the Mnemosyne panels are left pinned as he last moved them a week before. Saxl and Bing inherit an institution and an argument that stops in mid-sentence. He has published relatively little across a lifetime of colossal reading. What he leaves is a library shelved on a principle and an unfinished atlas of sixty-three panels. The method will reach English in the hands of the people who worked beside him, under conditions none of them can yet foresee.
suggested_refs: The photographic record of the panels in the state Warburg left them, October 1929

stops.name: Hamburg, the Ilandkoppel grave
stops.date_confidence: inferred burial date; the cemetery is attested, though several sources conflate it with the neighbouring municipal Ohlsdorf grounds, which have no Jewish section
stops.campa: He is buried in the Jewish cemetery at Ilandkoppel, beside the vast Ohlsdorf grounds, among the graves of the banking family whose firm he handed to his brother at thirteen. The stone is plain, nothing like the visual archive he leaves behind. Within four years the survivors will be arranging the escape of the library and then of themselves; within ten, this ground will need protecting from the state that surrounds it. He is spared the whole of it by four years exactly.
suggested_refs: The Jüdischer Friedhof Ilandkoppel, Hamburg, and the Warburg family stones

stops.name: Hamburg harbor, the library sails
stops.date_confidence: date attested; sources differ on whether the cargo left in one ship, named as the Hermia, or in two freighters
stops.campa: On the twelfth of December the whole Kulturwissenschaftliche Bibliothek Warburg leaves Hamburg for London: some sixty thousand volumes, twenty-five thousand photographs, the archive, the furniture, the Mnemosyne panels. Saxl and Bing have spent months moving a Jewish-founded institution out of a country nine months into the new regime, with Lord Lee of Fareham and Samuel Courtauld waiting at the other end. That same autumn, on a New York pier, Aby's kinsman Edward Warburg meets George Balanchine off the boat and pays for the school he will build.
suggested_refs: The December 1933 shipping manifests of the library's removal

stops.name: London, Thames House on Millbank
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the ships arrived in December 1933 but the installation dates to 1934, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The library is installed on the ground floor of Thames House on Millbank, fitted out for it by the architect Godfrey Samuel, a stopgap address for an institution with no country. The shelving principle survives the crossing intact; the good neighbor is reassembled in London exactly as it stood on the Heilwigstrasse. In 1937 it moves again, to the Imperial Institute buildings in South Kensington, where it will stay until 1958. Nothing has gone missing in either move, and scholars who followed it out of Germany use it daily.
suggested_refs: Thames House, Millbank, first London address of the Warburg library
sources: SCUP, 'Moving Memory: The Buildings of the Warburg Institute'

stops.name: London, Woburn Square
stops.date_confidence: attested for the incorporation into the University of London; the move to Woburn Square itself follows in 1958
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of November 1944, with the war not yet won, the library is formally incorporated into the University of London as the Warburg Institute. A private obsession begun as a boy's bargain over books becomes a public institution of the country that took it in, and in 1958 it moves into a building of its own on Woburn Square in Bloomsbury. The bank he refused at thirteen paid for every volume on those shelves. The regime that would have burned them never came within reach of a single one.
suggested_refs: The Charles Holden building for the Warburg Institute, Woburn Square, opened 1958
